transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-12
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~38 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex Gomez (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (BlueStripe CTO), Maya Patel (Eng Manager), Samir Khan (Data Eng)

Summary:
Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on streaming behavior, parameterization (max_tokens, temperature, stop, top_p), retry and backoff strategies, and a short discussion about data residency and HIPAA considerations for BlueStripe Health. Agreed to run small perf bench and share pricing options for burst/dedicated capacity.

Topics covered:
- Streaming: chunking, partial tokens, and client-side handling
- Parameters: token limits, temperature, stop sequences, truncation policies
- Retries: idempotency, retry-after, exponential backoff, fallbacks to shorter models
- Caching & batching: prefix/K-V cache, continuous batching tradeoffs
- Security: SOC2, KMS, data retention and HIPAA questions

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, good to see BlueStripe team. we're gonna run through a quick hosted cook-book style walkthrough — streaming, params, retries — maybe 30 ish minutes then q&a. Priya will show demo.
[00:18] Jordan (BlueStripe): yep thanks Alex, we only have 40 mins so if you can focus on streaming and error handling that'd be perfect. our product surfaces real-time chat for clinicians so latency matters.
[00:32] Priya (Redwood SE): great, i'll share my screen — starting with a simple chat.generate call, streaming enabled. i want to highlight how events come over as partial deltas, so your front-end can render tokens progressively. note: some transcribe err — sometimes the first delta includes punctuation fragments, that's normal.
[01:05] Maya (BlueStripe): quick clar, what happens if a stream drops mid-response? do we get an id or we re-request?
[01:12] Priya: good question — we surface a request_id per call. recommended pattern: on network hiccup, call our generative endpoint with the same request_id and a special resume flag or ask client to fetch the last committed token via the conversation API. for non-deterministic outputs we usually advise a conservative retry policy — replays can change the output.
[01:45] Samir (BlueStripe): so replays might create duplicates in the clinical note? that's a risk.
[01:52] Priya: right, that's why we also support deterministic seeds and response signatures for critical workflows, or you can use short-circuit fallbacks: if you detect a stream failure after N tokens, fall back to a smaller model that is faster and cheaper but consistent, or mark as partial and queue a server-side recheck.
[02:20] Alex: i'll pause — quick qualification, what's your target 95th percentile latency for a conversational turn?
[02:27] Jordan: under 500ms ideally for autocomplete snippets; for full note generation we can tolerate 2s - 3s but lower is better.
[02:35] Alex: good, that maps well to our hosted SLOs with streaming enabled. Priya, can you show param examples?
[02:40] Priya: yep, opening the playground snippet: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, stop sequences. Example: temperature 0.0 for deterministic extraction, 0.7 for creative suggestions. note: when streaming we emit tokens as they're decoded so temperature affects diversity in real time. also, we expose truncation_strategy — pre or post prompt truncation, useful when you have long KV cache footprints.
[03:18] Jordan: KV cache? can you explain again, i heard K-V cache but not totally clear.
[03:22] Priya: sure — K V cache is the model's key/value state for previous tokens; with streaming that cache is used to accelerate next-token gen. we also offer prefix caching on the service side so repeated prompts can hit cache and avoid recomputation. some customers call it K-V cash in transcrip, haha.
[03:48] Maya: are there limits on cache size or TTL?
[03:52] Priya: yes TTL is configurable per route, default 30 min for shorter sessions but you can extend for longer conversations. limits depend on model variant and sequence length; we'll share the cache sizing guide.
[04:12] Alex: moving to retries — typical pattern is immediate try once then exponential backoff with jitter, plus a circuit-breaker if you exceed X failures. Priya, show HTTP status mappings.
[04:22] Priya: on hosted API, you'll see 429 when rate limits or quotas hit, 503 for transient infra issues, and 5xx for server errors. recommended client-side logic: on 429/503 -> exponential backoff + retry up to 3 times for idempotent ops; for non-idempotent generative calls, prefer resume token or mark partial. also we provide 'retry-after' header for nicer backoff.
[05:00] Samir: what's the idempotency token look like? do we pass it as header?
[05:04] Priya: you can pass idempotency_key in the request body or header. if you pass the same key and the service already completed the request, we'll return the stored response. if the call failed mid-stream we'll indicate partial state.
[05:25] Jordan: cost question — does streaming cost more per token?
[05:30] Alex: cost model is per output token for the hosted API; streaming itself doesn't add cost, but maintaining longer context and KV cache can add memory overhead which can drive you to larger model configs. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization (e.g., int8) or shorter context profiles to reduce unit cost.
[05:56] Maya: we are in healthcare — HIPAA is a big one. do you keep logs? how long? is data encrypted with customer KMS?
[06:05] Priya: we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for Private deployments; for hosted we offer envelope encryption and SOC 2 controls. data retention is configurable — default short retention for logs but you can opt-in to longer retention for debugging. for HIPAA you can go Private or dedicated with BAA — Alex will follow up with the compliance pack.
[06:40] Jordan: so hosted is possible if we can sign a BAA?
[06:44] Alex: yes, hosted can be covered under a BAA if legal signs off; many healthcare customers prefer Dedicated or Private for stricter network controls. we'll send details.
[07:00] Priya: demo time — i'm going to simulate a 2-turn convo, stream tokens, then force a network drop to show resume behavior. watching the console...
[07:18] [screen share: terminal output, streaming chunked JSON events]
[07:25] Priya: see each chunk has token_delta and cursor_position, request_id, and an optional resume_cursor. if the client reconnects we can provide resume_cursor to continue.
[07:45] Maya: if we resume and the model produced something different the second time, how do we reconcile?
[07:50] Priya: good point — we surface a response_signature that you can verify against a stored hash; for deterministic ends use temperature 0 and seed. otherwise, server-side reconciliation rules are needed — e.g., prefer the first successful complete response and drop later duplicates.
[08:15] Alex: question to the team — are you planning long form note generations or short assistance?
[08:22] Jordan: mix — short autocompletes in UI and long summaries overnight. latency for UI paths is priority.
[08:30] Priya: for UI short paths, keep max_tokens low (e.g., 64-256) and use continuous batching on server side; Redwood runtime will batch small requests to improve throughput without adding much latency. for long form, prefer async generation and then store embedding for retrieval.
[09:05] Samir: continuous batching — does that add delay while waiting for the batch window?
[09:09] Priya: minimal, you can configure target latency and batch size; by default we use very small windows (10-20ms) for low latency. if your 95th p95 is strict, you can disable batching for that route.
[09:30] Maya: curious about model fallbacks — you mentioned using smaller models as graceful degradation?
[09:36] Priya: yes, smart routing rules let you prefer low-latency variants first, then fallback to larger models if quality is needed or vice versa depending on cost. you can set policy by route: prefer latency, prefer quality, or cost-saver. if a model is busy, requests automatically route to compatible variants.
[10:00] Jordan: any risk of hallucination increase when falling back to smaller models?
[10:04] Priya: generally smaller models may hallucinate more on open-ended tasks; for extraction tasks it's often fine. Redwood Optimize can run evals against your prompt sets and recommend which model/quant profile keeps accuracy within thresholds. note: we call out any regression in the console.
[10:30] Alex: let's talk about partial responses stored in audit logs — are those considered customer data for retention?
[10:36] Priya: yes. we treat all request/response artifacts as customer data; retention policies apply. for hosted we can set masked logging and PII redaction, but for full HIPAA workloads we recommend Private or Dedicated.
[11:00] Maya: what's the SDK behavior for languages? we use node + kotlin backend.
[11:06] Priya: we have SDKs for python, node, and java/golang examples. node has streaming helper that emits 'token' events; kotlin can use server-sent events. we'll share code samples.
[11:30] Samir: earlier you mentioned quota throttles — how do we handle bursty traffic from clinicians during midday?
[11:36] Alex: reserved capacity (Dedicated) is best for predictable burst, hosted supports burst capacity but with soft limits; you can also set client-side queueing and graceful fallbacks. for critical SLAs choose Dedicated or hybrid with reserved commit.
[12:05] Jordan: do you have pre-wired canary rollouts? we want to A/B a new prompt template with 5% of traffic.
[12:12] Priya: yes, rollout policies in console support canary percentages, automatic rollback on error rate or quality regressions, and traffic splitting by route or user segment.
[12:40] Alex: let's demo retry-after in practice — i'm going to trigger a simulated rate limit and show how header looks.
[12:50] [demo shows 429 response and Retry-After: 3s header]
[13:00] Priya: recommended client pattern: on 429 respect retry-after with jitter, and optionally backoff exponentially. for streaming we suggest reattach logic that requests only missing tokens using resume cursor.
[13:28] Maya: ok that helps — we're worried about duplicate notes written by clinicians, can we implement server-side dedupe?
[13:35] Priya: yes often done by having the client generate a conversation_id + message_id and server supports idempotency; also storing response_signature to ensure duplication is detected.
[13:58] Samir: do you provide retention logs for auditing? need to show to compliance.
[14:02] Alex: yes audit logs available, retention configurable per plan. Priya will attach compliance pack.
[14:20] Jordan: you mentioned model quantization earlier — does that impact latency?
[14:24] Priya: quantization (int8/4) reduces memory and often improves throughput; sometimes slight quality delta. Redwood Optimize will suggest a quant profile per workload and run evals to show delta vs token savings.
[14:50] Maya: can we try a quick throughput test? maybe 50 parallel short prompts.
[14:56] Priya: we can kick off a small bench in the next email exchange — for now i'll show sample results from a 50-concurrent run: p50 180ms, p95 620ms on hosted with streaming and small model. remember this varies by region and model.
[15:28] Jordan: region — we need EU/NA data residency. can we pin region?
[15:33] Alex: yes, hosted supports regions and routing by policy; Dedicated and Private gives you single-region isolation. we'll note EU region for your account.
[15:50] Maya: security question — SSO and SAML for team access?
[15:54] Priya: yes, SAML/SSO and RBAC are supported. audit logs show per-token breakouts and user actions.
[16:10] Samir: any notable gotchas integrating with our existing event pipeline? we push messages into kafka then call APIs.
[16:16] Priya: standard approach is to have a small stateless worker that handles retry/attach and posts results to kafka; avoid doing heavy blocking on the request path. we also offer webhook callbacks for async jobs.
[16:40] Alex: wrapping up — Jordan any blockers to start a pilot?
[16:45] Jordan: two things — HIPAA scoping and a short perf bench we can run with our payloads. if those look good we can kickoff pilot.
[16:55] Alex: perfect, next steps: Priya sends bench script and sample payloads, Alex sends pricing and BAA/compliance pack. Jordan will reply with security contact and confirm pilot scope.
[17:12] Maya: one last question — what's a typical billing cadence for hosted? monthly with usage spikes billed next cycle?
[17:18] Alex: monthly invoicing by default; for Dedicated we do monthly committed spend with overage. we'll include billing examples.
[17:35] Jordan: thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[17:38] Alex: thanks — we'll follow up via email with artifacts and schedule the pilot kickoff.

Closing notes:
- Artifacts to attach: hosted pricing PDF, compliance pack (SOC2, BAA template), bench script, sample payloads, SDK code snippets, cache sizing guide.
- Agreed pilot goals: validate UI latency <500ms p95 for short prompts, verify HIPAA scoping and BAA, and run 1k request perf test on sample flows.

End of transcript (approx 38 minutes).
